notes.1a: Most candidates labelled the graph axes correctly and drew them the right way round, choosing a suitable scale. Some candidates ignored the advice that they did not need to begin the axes at the origin and chose a scale that resulted in the plots occupying too little of the graph grid. Plotting was generally accurate. Candidates should use neat crosses for the plots, or neatly circled dots so that the accuracy of the plotting can be read clearly. Many candidates drew a well-judged straight line but some drew a ‘dot-to-dot’ line whilst others drew a straight line that did not match the plots, usually by forcing the line to go through the origin or false origin.
notes.1b: Here candidates needed to clearly show the triangle method on the graph, with a large triangle using at least half the distance between the extreme plots. Many candidates achieved this.
notes.1c: The value of W 1 was expected to be correctly calculated and given to 2 or 3 significant figures with the unit N.
notes.1d: Candidates were expected to use their experience of practical work to record an aspect of the experiment that proved difficult in practice. Many sensibly chose to comment on the difficulty of achieving balance or the problem of the loads obscuring the reading on the rule.
notes.1e: Here candidates were expected to record 113 g.
notes.1fi: Few candidates successfully converted from kg to g to obtain the answer 1.13 N.
notes.1fii: Here candidates were effectively asked to explain their understanding of “within the limits of experimental accuracy”. Credit was awarded for a sensible explanation that matched their own values of W and W . 1 2
notes.2a: Most candidates recorded the current to at least 2 decimal places.
notes.2b: V / l values were expected to be correct and given to a consistent 2 significant figures or consistent 3 significant figures. A significant number of candidates did not complete the column heading.
notes.2ci: and (ii) Here candidates were required to make a judgement based on their own results. The justification needed to be clear and consistent with the results to gain credit.
notes.2d: Most candidates used the correct information from the table, calculated R successfully and gave the result to 2 or 3 significant figures with the unit Ω . Credit was available for significant figures and unit if the calculation was incorrect. Some candidates used the wrong information, for example using the 100 (cm) in place of the value of V at 100 cm.
notes.2e: Many candidates answered this correctly. However, a variety of impractical suggestions were seen which could not be credited.
notes.2f: Many candidates drew the correct symbol with care. Some candidates drew the symbol for a thermistor.
notes.3bi: Most candidates gave the correct units, s and °C.
notes.3bii: Here candidates were required to make a judgement based on the readings in the table.
notes.3biii: The justification needed to be clear. Initial and final readings, or differences in those readings, needed to be quoted and the small difference noted in order to obtain full credit.
notes.3ci: Stronger candidates were able to analyse the question well and gave relevant answers concentrating on providing a shiny can and a black-painted beaker. However, some candidates gave answers that were not appropriate for the question as it had been set. This usually resulted in candidates suggesting precautions rather than identifying changes.
notes.3cii: Many candidates made sensible suggestions here.
notes.3d: Candidates were expected to suggest a relevant practical precaution here. Many chose to refer to perpendicular viewing of the thermometer scale.
